summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for setting up and configuring Banyan VINES over PPP. It is now historic.

subtitle: Control protocol for running Banyan VINES over point-to-point links.

tldr.problem: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) needed a control protocol for establishing and configuring Banyan VINES, a network protocol used in enterprise environments, over point-to-point links.
tldr.mechanism: BVCP follows the same message exchange mechanism as PPP's Link Control Protocol, using configuration request/response packets to negotiate network layer options specific to VINES.
tldr.outcome: BVCP allows PPP to transport VINES traffic with negotiated parameters for routing, fragmentation, and broadcast handling. The RFC is now historic.

today: RFC 1661 defined PPP, and RFC 1763 is a historic specification. Banyan VINES is no longer in active use, and this protocol has not been updated.

sections.title: Introduction to PPP and BVCP
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links like phone lines. PPP has three main parts: a method for encapsulating different network protocols, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for setting up the physical link, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring each network layer protocol.

The Banyan VINES Control Protocol (BVCP) is an NCP that enables PPP to transport Banyan VINES, a network protocol used in enterprise environments. Before any VINES data can flow, PPP must first establish the physical link using LCP, and then BVCP must negotiate and enable the VINES layer.
sections.eli5: PPP is a way to send any kind of network traffic over a simple point-to-point link. BVCP is the rulebook for one specific type of traffic: Banyan VINES.

sections.title: BVCP Operation and Message Exchange
sections.content:
BVCP uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP, using Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, and Terminate-Ack packets. BVCP packets are encapsulated with protocol type 0x8035 (Banyan VINES Control Protocol) in the PPP frame.

BVCP packets may only be exchanged after PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase, meaning the physical link is established and any required authentication or quality checking has completed. Once BVCP reaches the Opened state, VINES datagrams can be transmitted using protocol type 0x0035 in the PPP frame. The maximum VINES datagram length is limited by the negotiated Maximum Receive Unit (MRU) of the PPP link.
sections.eli5: BVCP is a back-and-forth conversation between the two ends of the link, where each side says what it needs for VINES to work properly. Once both sides agree, VINES traffic can flow.

sections.title: Configuration Options
sections.content:
BVCP allows negotiation of four configuration options specific to VINES traffic:

BV-NS-RTP-Link-Type negotiates whether the Non-Sequenced Routing Update Protocol (NS-RTP) should treat the link as a LAN type (sending full routing table updates every 90 seconds) or a WAN type (sending full updates only for the first three intervals, then only changes). The default is WAN type.

BV-FRP negotiates whether to use the VINES Fragmentation Protocol, which prepends a two-octet header to allow reassembly of large packets. This is needed only when the PPP MRU is less than 1484 bytes.

BV-RTP negotiates whether to send VINES routing update packets. On static dial-up lines, RTP can be suppressed to conserve bandwidth. BV-Suppress-Broadcast allows clients to request that servers not send broadcast packets (except VINES ARP and RTP), reducing link traffic.
sections.eli5: Before sending VINES data, the two sides negotiate what special rules to use: how to send routing updates, whether to split large messages, whether to send route updates at all, and how much broadcast traffic to send.

sections.title: VINES Data Transfer and Compatibility
sections.content:
Once BVCP is in the Opened state, VINES datagrams are sent as single VINES packets encapsulated in PPP frames. The RFC notes that VINES supports an Address Resolution Protocol (VINES ARP) used for address assignment, which is fully supported over BVCP. However, the VINES Echo Protocol used for testing connectivity in LAN environments is not supported over point-to-point links.

The protocol relies on concepts from Banyan's VINES specification, specifically RFC-referenced document VINES Protocol Definition. Configuration negotiation happens separately on each side of the link, allowing asymmetric behavior where each end can request different treatment for traffic it receives.
sections.eli5: Once the link is ready, actual VINES messages travel back and forth. Some VINES features work over the link, but some LAN-specific tools for testing connections do not.
